content:
Jointly-signed owners were once refused entry; staff said only one person could enter

At the Tin Fai Community Hall, residents began entering from 9 am, some arriving by tour bus. At around 10 am, when several jointly-signed owners tried to enter, staff insisted that only one person could go in, with another allowed in only if there were spare seats. This sparked dissatisfaction among the owners, who gathered noisily at the hall entrance: "Pulling off all these tricks… you have so many venues… you've done the math," and "It's only a thousand-plus households, acting so furtively."

When a reporter tried to film, police officers stopped them and directed them to a press area outside the hall, saying no one was allowed to stay or take photos at the scene. Some on-site staff told owners that it had already been stated online that only one owner could enter. However, checking the information, Hop On (合安) only stated that due to venue capacity limits, each unit could only be represented by the owner or an authorised representative, without specifying the number of people. The owners in question were eventually all allowed in before the meeting began.

At the Tin Fai Community Hall, some jointly-signed owners were at first refused entry, with staff saying the venue was limited and only one person could go in, with another allowed in only if there were spare seats; those unable to enter queued up nearby to wait.

Mr Mak of Wang Yan Court: just a work report meeting, not satisfactory

About two hours after the meeting began and after the first round of voting, at around 1 pm, a small number of residents left, including high-floor owners Mr and Mrs Mak of Wang Yan Court and several other residents. As one of the owners who had co-signed to convene the meeting, Mr Mak candidly said he had no expectations beforehand: "We came just to see how they'd hold this so-called owners' meeting." The result was exactly as he had imagined: "This isn't an owners' meeting, it's just a work report meeting."

Mimicking the way officials speak, Mr Mak described the meeting's content as "not satisfactory": "They couldn't deliver what we asked for, they deleted the agenda items we requested—tell me if that's satisfactory or not?" He was also unhappy: "Everything they say is nothing to do with them, just like government officials talking—saying we can't do it, this is the government's job. But you're our agent, aren't you? Shouldn't you be telling the government what we ask for? All they say is we can't do it, what can we do about it." Nevertheless, he said this was expected, noting that Hop On was also appointed by the government.

Said there was a commotion at the meeting: if this were a conference hall, there'd be a riot

Mr and Mrs Mak questioned whether Hop On had "faked the numbers" on attendance, and also criticised the fact that during the first round of questions, only one person was allowed to ask a question at the Tin Shui Wai venue: "Lots of people wanted to ask but couldn't, and the answers were evasive." Residents in the hall would heckle from time to time. "We've endured for seven months, bottled it up for seven months—wouldn't you be worked up?" he said. "If this were a conference hall, there'd be a riot."

Mr and Mrs Mak are original residents of Wang Fuk Court. Because they felt the information was unclear, they have not yet submitted the acquisition intent form: "We want to see more clearly." They also admitted that returning to Tai Po to live was "just a dream for us," but at present there was "nothing we can plan for." They hoped to be able to go back upstairs to pack again, "taking everything we can," saying their home was still in good condition and they had only retrieved less than a third of their belongings so far: "Only two visits of six hours each—how much can you take?"

Seventy-year-old grandmother of Wang Tai Court chooses to sell her title: no choice, have to accept it

A seventy-year-old grandmother living in Wang Tai Court also left at around 1:30 pm, saying "I heard what I most wanted to hear, so I left." She said she was most concerned about whether the remaining management fees and other sums for the estate would be returned to owners after selling the title; Hop On said at the meeting that "they would give it back to us." As for insurance compensation, she said "if there is, there is; if there isn't, there isn't," and was not worried about not receiving insurance payouts after selling her flat, joking: "I trust the government. The government shouldn't cheat us, right? Still picking food out of a beggar's pocket? They should pay what they should, and not charge what they shouldn't."

The grandmother is currently living in transitional housing at Hung Shui Kiu. She said her first choice was originally to go to Tai Po for the meeting, planning "to look up some friends and have dim sum," but "I couldn't get a slot so I came here instead." It has been nearly eight months since the fire. She said at first it was "nothing much," but "the longer I live here, the more unhappy I become." "After all, you don't have your own home…the space is small, nothing like the old flat, it's twice as bad, and there seems to be no room for activities around here." She therefore hopes to be able to go back upstairs as soon as possible.

A resident since Wang Fuk Court was built, the grandmother has signed the agreement to sell her title. Having to sell a home of more than 40 years, she said "there's no choice, you have to accept it," and laughed wryly: "What can you do if you don't sell? If you absolutely refuse to sell, what's the point of holding on to the title? You have nowhere to live. You have to be realistic."

Four tour buses and one minibus were parked at the scene, ferrying residents away, with help from care teams. The press area was set up more than ten metres from where residents boarded, separated by railings.

Mr Yuen of Wang Shing Court: at least put on a show, get the reports out

Mr Yuen, a resident of Wang Kin Court, told reporters after the meeting that he had no expectations for it, and ultimately got no answers: "It was just the same things they'd said before." He said residents most cared about the inspection reports, wanting to understand why all eight blocks had to be demolished: "Everyone wants to know why our home is gone, but no one can give an answer." Hop On also said "it's nothing to do with them."

Regarding the inspection report, Hop On said there would be typhoon and rainy seasons ahead, and they had to wait for the authorities to check safety conditions: "Everyone wait a while, once they've done it they might announce it to everyone." This sparked heckling from several residents. Mr Yuen said, although everyone knows why they want to "take back the whole piece of land," "at least everyone should put on a show and get the reports out. But they can't even get them—they say the typhoons and rain mean they can't retrieve the reports. There's nothing we can do, we're just ordinary citizens, there's nothing more to say."

Mr Yuen, a resident of Wang Kin Court

As for the meeting, Mr Yuen candidly said, "I don't feel anything about it, I expected as much. I think sitting in there was just a process." He has not yet signed the intent form, saying there are still many considerations, including how to handle things for his parents and children: "It's not something that can be solved just by selling at once." It has been nearly eight months since the fire. He said, "These eight months of suffering, you have to sort it out yourself the whole way…the whole family suffers, but we have to face it."

Asked what he would like to say to the government or Hop On, Mr Yuen replied calmly: "I think whatever we say is pointless, because they think they're doing great, arrangements are great. What we say—everyone's been saying it all along. Whether they like hearing it or not, I think we've already expressed it all. So…we really have to thank them."

Ms Wong of Wang Chi Court

Wang Chi Court resident questions selling flat without knowing insurance payout

Ms Wong, a resident of Wang Chi Court, told reporters after the meeting that she felt helpless. She said the agenda items they had hoped to discuss were deleted, and the whole meeting followed Hop On's arrangements and was controlled by them. She said she had originally hoped to find out whether the HK$2 billion fire insurance would be paid out if the buildings were not rebuilt or repaired; a representative from Taiping Insurance said at the meeting that "if it should be paid, it will be paid," but the actual arrangements were unknown and still pending. She questioned whether, without knowing the insurance payout, "we have to sell our titles before 31 August—has the order been reversed?" She said normally the compensation amount should be calculated first, and only then would one decide whether to sell.

Ms Wong has not yet signed the acquisition intent form, saying she has many questions and wants clear information before deciding. She stressed that Wang Chi Court had not been burnt and was perfectly safe: "Why can't I go home?…What ordinance, what department, is stopping us from going home to get our things?" Residents asked several times at the meeting but got no answer. The meeting also resolved to convene another general meeting within two months. Though she has no expectations, she still believes one should be held as soon as possible and should not wait until after 31 August, when residents sell their titles. She also hopes the deadline for selling flats will be extended.

Situation inside the Tin Shui Wai venue (footage provided by owners on site)

Uncomfortable with the broadcast arrangements, making the process run poorly

Regarding the meeting's arrangements, Ms Wong candidly said she felt "very uncomfortable." She said in previous meetings all residents attended in person, but now they were split across different places. At the three venues everyone was "just watching a screen," and you couldn't even see what was happening at the other venues. Whenever she wanted to ask a question or clarify something with the chair, she had to rely on staff present to relay it, often without success. The process was also not smooth—taking turns to draw lots and ask questions wasted a lot of time, similar to the last briefing. She believes that if residents could communicate and discuss in the same venue, the process would be smoother and require less manpower and resources, and she hopes Hop On will improve this next time.

Although dissatisfied with the meeting's arrangements, Ms Wong described the reunion with fellow residents, being able to "discuss things together," as somewhat heartening: "At last we've had the first meeting. Although this meeting seems to have yielded few answers, seeing the residents, being able to talk things through together—that feels good."

Mr Tsang of Wang Yan Court

Mr Tsang of Wang Yan Court: endless run-around, it's just a show

Mr Tsang, an owner who has lived in Wang Yan Court for a year and a half, described the whole meeting on his way out as "just a show." The agenda was decided by Hop On and owners' questions went unanswered: "A lot of it was just taking you on a run-around." Particularly on insurance, he said residents were worried whether, after selling their titles, insurance would pay out to the government. The chair did not answer, "just kept going around in circles."

Mr Tsang does not plan to sell his title for now. He said the government requires residents to sell their titles before 31 August, otherwise legal action will be taken, but the insurance company says it will decide on payouts only after the government issues an investigation report, while the government says it will issue the report only after the titles are sold: "Everyone's pushing it back and forth, no decision can be made." He hopes the deadline for selling flats can be extended, or the report issued sooner.

Regarding the meeting's resolution to hold a general meeting within two months, Mr Tsang is worried that if the meeting is held only after 31 August, the government will already hold most of the titles and be able to decide the direction and content of the meeting, with residents having "no say over many things." He is also unhappy that residents have been "scattered all over" different places, making communication difficult, and believes the government is "very worried about us uniting."

Mr Li of Wang Tao Court authorisation fails; over an hour of confusion before being allowed in

Mr Li of Wang Tao Court likewise felt that this meeting "won't help much" and could not answer owners' questions: "Everyone came with uncertain thoughts, and after this owners' meeting nothing has changed, there's still a lot we don't know." He said he felt that "after selling the title, a lot of things you can't follow up on anymore," including insurance and the rights of owners' meetings, and he also believes that by the next meeting the government will already hold most of the titles, making attendance pointless.

Mr Li was authorised by family members to attend and had submitted all documents before the deadline, but was notified the day before the meeting that his authorisation had failed, with no reason given; calls to the Hop On hotline also yielded no answer. He returned to the venue at 10 am today, and staff again did not mention why the authorisation failed but checked his documents. After over an hour of back-and-forth, he was finally allowed into the venue at 11:15 am.

The Tin Shui Wai vote-monitoring lawyer did not disclose his name or law firm when pressed by residents, and did not respond to reporters' questions as he left the hall.

Tin Shui Wai vote-monitoring lawyer refuses to identify himself

Additionally, lawyers were present to monitor the vote-counting at each venue during the owners' meeting. More than one resident mentioned that the lawyer at the Tin Shui Wai venue did not identify himself at the time, and only when pressed by residents did the host point out a certain man as the lawyer. He said he did not have a business card and refused to disclose his name or law firm. Residents pressed him on his identity, and Hop On said they would look into it, but in the end his identity was never confirmed. Mr Cheng, an owner of Wang Tai Court, described the situation as very bizarre, questioning "whether everyone's just putting on a show and casually saying he's a lawyer monitoring the vote." The man walked out of the hall at nearly 5 pm. When reporters asked whether he was a lawyer, his name, and which law firm he belonged to, he did not respond and immediately turned back into the hall.
